strategy.approach: Spend the first three days on the vertex formula $h=-\frac{b}{2a}$, converting between forms, and range and min/max, since they drive most of the exam. Use the last three days on intercepts and word problems, and check the odd-numbered exercises against the answer key.
objectives: Recognize the characteristics of a parabola: vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts, and whether it opens up or down.
Write a quadratic function in general form $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ and in standard (vertex) form $f(x)=a(x-h)^2+k$, and convert between the two.
Find the domain and range of a quadratic function.
Determine a quadratic function's minimum or maximum value.
Solve application problems that ask for a minimum or maximum (area, revenue, projectile height).
Find the x-intercepts and the y-intercept of a quadratic function, also with the quadratic formula.

topics.title: Vertex, axis of symmetry and converting forms
topics.why: Almost every exam question starts by finding the vertex with $h=-\frac{b}{2a}$, $k=f(h)$ or by rewriting $f$ in vertex form. This covers objectives 1 and 2.
topics.skipCost: Without the vertex you cannot do the min/max, range or application questions either, so you lose points across the whole exam.

topics.title: Domain, range and minimum/maximum value
topics.why: These are short, quick-scoring questions: the sign of $a$ tells you min or max, and $k$ gives you the range. This covers objectives 3 and 4.
topics.skipCost: You give away easy points on questions that take under five minutes each.

topics.title: x- and y-intercepts with the quadratic formula
topics.why: Objective 6 explicitly asks for the quadratic formula. You need $f(0)$ for the y-intercept, $f(x)=0$ for the x-intercepts, and the discriminant tells you how many x-intercepts there are.
topics.skipCost: You cannot sketch graphs, and you cannot answer 'when does it hit the ground' in projectile problems.

topics.title: Area and revenue optimization
topics.why: Word problems with fencing or price and demand are typical high-value questions. You set up the function, then take its vertex. This covers objective 5.
topics.skipCost: Word problems usually carry many points, and you would lose the setup marks completely.

topics.title: Projectile height
topics.why: The maximum height comes from the vertex and the landing time from the positive root. This combines objectives 5 and 6 in one question.
topics.skipCost: You risk losing a complete multi-part question (time of maximum height, maximum height, landing time).

topics.title: Equation from the vertex and a point, or from a table
topics.why: You put the vertex into $a(x-h)^2+k$, solve for $a$ using a second point, then expand to general form. This tests objectives 1 and 2.
topics.skipCost: You lose the 'find the equation' questions, which are routine once you have practised them.

topics.title: Review: factoring and completing the square
topics.why: This is a supporting skill: factoring is the fastest way to find intercepts, and completing the square leads to vertex form. It is rarely asked on its own.
topics.skipCost: You lose a little speed on intercept questions, but the quadratic formula still gets you the answer.

questions.explain: The function is in standard form with vertex $(3,5)$ and $a=-2<0$, so the parabola opens downward with a maximum of 5. The range is $(-\infty,k]=(-\infty,5]$.

questions.prompt: Find the domain and range of $f(x)=x^2-6x+11$.
questions.answer: Domain: all real numbers, $(-\infty,\infty)$. Vertex: $h=-\frac{-6}{2\cdot 1}=3$, $f(3)=9-18+11=2$. Since $a=1>0$, the range is $[2,\infty)$.
questions.rubric: 1 point for the domain as all real numbers. 1 point for finding the vertex $x$-value 3 and $f(3)=2$. 1 point for the range $[2,\infty)$ with a closed bracket, because $a>0$.
questions.explain: Any real number can be the input, so the domain is all real numbers. With $a>0$ the parabola has a minimum at the vertex, $f(3)=2$, so the outputs are all values $\ge 2$.

choices: It has a minimum value of 11 at $x=2$.
It has a maximum value of 11 at $x=2$.
It has a maximum value of 2 at $x=11$.
It has a minimum value of $-1$ at $x=0$.
questions.answer: It has a maximum value of 11 at $x=2$.
questions.explain: Since $a=-3<0$, the parabola opens downward and has a maximum. The vertex is at $x=-\frac{12}{2(-3)}=2$, and $f(2)=-12+24-1=11$.

questions.prompt: Find the minimum value of $f(x)=2x^2+8x+3$ and the input value where it occurs.
questions.answer: $h=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 2}=-2$ and $f(-2)=8-16+3=-5$. The minimum value is $-5$, and it occurs at $x=-2$.
questions.rubric: 1 point for finding $x=-2$ with $h=-\frac{b}{2a}$. 1 point for $f(-2)=-5$. 1 point for stating that it is a minimum because $a>0$.
questions.explain: The output at the vertex is the extreme value. With $a=2>0$ the parabola opens upward, so $f(-2)=-5$ is the minimum.

questions.prompt: A quadratic function has range $(-\infty,-4]$. What follows from this?
choices: The parabola opens upward and has a minimum value of $-4$.
The parabola opens downward and its maximum occurs at $x=-4$.
The parabola opens downward and its maximum value is $-4$.
questions.answer: The parabola opens downward and its maximum value is $-4$.
questions.explain: A range bounded above, $(-\infty,k]$, means $a<0$ and the parabola opens downward. The bound $k=-4$ is the output (the $y$-coordinate) at the vertex, not the input.
